We conduct empirical evaluations of ReAct and state-of-the-art baselines on four diverse benchmarks:
question answering (HotPotQA, Yang et al., 2018), fact veriﬁcation (Fever, Thorne et al., 2018),
text-based game (ALFWorld, Shridhar et al., 2020b), and webpage navigation (WebShop, Yao
et al., 2022). For HotPotQA and Fever, with access to a Wikipedia API that the model can interact
with, ReAct outperforms vanilla action generation models while being competitive with chain-of-
thought reasoning (CoT) (Wei et al., 2022). The best approach overall is a combination of ReAct
and CoT that allows for the use of both internal knowledge and externally obtained information
during reasoning. On ALFWorld and WebShop, two or even one-shot ReAct prompting is able
to outperform imitation or reinforcement learning methods trained with 103 ∼105 task instances,
with an absolute improvement of 34% and 10% in success rates respectively. We also demonstrate
the importance of sparse, versatile reasoning in decision making by showing consistent advantages
over controlled baselines with actions only. Besides general applicability and performance boost,
the combination of reasoning and acting also contributes to model interpretability, trustworthiness,
and diagnosability across all domains, as humans can readily distinguish information from model’s
internal knowledge versus external environments, as well as inspect reasoning traces to understand
the decision basis of model actions.

To summarize, our key contributions are the following: (1) we introduce ReAct, a novel prompt-
based paradigm to synergize reasoning and acting in language models for general task solving; (2) we
perform extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks to showcase the advantage of ReAct in a
few-shot learning setup over prior approaches that perform either reasoning or action generation in
isolation; (3) we present systematic ablations and analysis to understand th", "version_id": "arxiv:2210.03629:v3", "work_id": "arxiv:2210.03629"}, {"end": 4000, "material_id": "mat-2b7a38f3cfa1449f7728f044688ca2c2", "page": 3, "parser_revision": "workspace-pymupdf-1.28.0-text-sort-v1-selected-pages-v1", "scope": "excerpt", "section": null, "source_hash": "sha256:f285b0971ae4a790e402fb93966bed3adde2cf0a04977d08b2b40d6ab0cace69", "span_id": "span-e938044ecb931aff97360bd1fe27f3df", "start": 2000, "text": "e importance of acting in
reasoning tasks, and reasoning in interactive tasks; (4) we analyze the limitations of ReAct under the
prompting setup (i.e. limited support of reasoning and acting behaviors), and perform initial ﬁnetuning
experiments showing the potential of ReAct to improve with additional training data. Scaling up
ReAct to train and operate on more tasks and combining it with complementary paradigms like
reinforcement learning could further unlock the potential of large language models.

2  REAC T: SYNERGIZING REASONING + ACTING

Consider a general setup of an agent interacting with an environment for task solving. At time
step t, an agent receives an observation ot ∈O from the environment and takes an action at ∈A
following some policy π(at|ct), where ct = (o1, a1, · · · , ot−1, at−1, ot) is the context to the agent.
Learning a policy is challenging when the mapping ct 7→at is highly implicit and requires extensive
computation. For example, the agent shown in Figure 1(1c) is unable to generate the correct ﬁnal
action (Act 4) to ﬁnish the QA task as it requires complex reasoning over the trajectory context
(Question, Act 1-3, Obs 1-3). Similarly, the agent shown in Figure 1(2a) fails to comprehend from the
context that sinkbasin 1 does not contain peppershaker 1, thus keep producing hallucinating actions.
The idea of ReAct is simple: we augment the agent’s action space to Aˆ = A ∪L, where L is the
space of language. An action ˆat ∈L in the language space, which we will refer to as a thought or a
reasoning trace, does not affect the external environment, thus leading to no observation feedback.
Instead, a thought ˆat aims to compose useful information by reasoning over the current context ct,
and update the context ct+1 = (ct, ˆat) to support future reasoning or acting. As shown in Figure 1,
there could be various types of useful thoughts, e.g. decomposing task goals and create action plans
(2b, Act 1; 1d, Thought 1), injecting commonsense knowledge rele", "version_id": "arxiv:2210.03629:v3", "work_id": "arxiv:2210.03629"}, {"end": 5255, "material_id": "mat-2b7a38f3cfa1449f7728f044688ca2c2", "page": 3, "parser_revision": "workspace-pymupdf-1.28.0-text-sort-v1-selected-pages-v1", "scope": "excerpt", "section": null, "source_hash": "sha256:f285b0971ae4a790e402fb93966bed3adde2cf0a04977d08b2b40d6ab0cace69", "span_id": "span-e505ce9b7c0a17016f4e22e8caea7810", "start": 4000, "text": "vant to task solving (2b, Act 1),
extracting important parts from observations (1d, Thought2, 4), track progress and transit action plans
(2b, Act 8), handle exceptions and adjust action plans (1d, Thought 3), and so on.

However, as the language space L is unlimited, learning in this augmented action space is difﬁcult
and requires strong language priors. In this paper, we mainly focus on the setup where a frozen
large language model, PaLM-540B (Chowdhery et al., 2022)1, is prompted with few-shot in-context
examples to generate both domain-speciﬁc actions and free-form language thoughts for task solving
(Figure 1 (1d), (2b)). Each in-context example is a human trajectory of actions, thoughts, and
environment observations to solve a task instance (see Appendix C). For the tasks where reasoning is
of primary importance (Figure 1(1)), we alternate the generation of thoughts and actions so that the
task-solving trajectory consists of multiple thought-action-observation steps. In contrast, for decision
making tasks that potentially involve a large number of actions (Figure 1(2)), thoughts only need to

messages.content: {"kind": "summary", "private_context": {"history": false, "notes": false, "profile": false}, "sources": [{"complete": true, "content_hash": "sha256:a1e2d03e8e9d1c84b615b075c16a309c69499e3fa466b8502a8ae63cc36aca32", "material_id": "mat-54f2f6e0645f499458d5030d06e35a59", "offset_basis": "page-local Unicode code points; end exclusive", "page_count": null, "page_numbers": null, "parser_revision": "workspace-plain-text-v1", "quality": "text_extracted", "scope": "abstract", "source_hash": "sha256:2b307ec864315d90d5e828786c2505fff1feda8837559b7e8601961ea9717759", "spans": [{"end": 875, "material_id": "mat-54f2f6e0645f499458d5030d06e35a59", "page": null, "parser_revision": "workspace-plain-text-v1", "scope": "abstract", "section": "abstract", "source_hash": "sha256:2b307ec864315d90d5e828786c2505fff1feda8837559b7e8601961ea9717759", "span_id": "span-3fd278aadaa92873179ed21c075ab368", "start": 0, "text": "Recursive textual memory can carry earlier errors into later updates, yet task performance alone does not establish memory reliability. We define self-consistency bias as the persistence of incorrect claims already present in the incoming memory. We present KEEPER, a comparative analysis of four auxiliary objectives along information-content and update-sensitivity axes within a shared recursive interface, examining how supervision targets relate to agent performance. Among evaluated conditions, reward-related prediction achieve the highest task performance before and after offline reinforcement learning, outperforming joint supervision. A claim-level analysis of one baseline trajectory documents error persistence despite corrective observations. Together, these analyses motivate evaluating error persistence and valid-information retention alongside task outcomes.", "version_id": "arxiv:2610.41482:v1:metadata-e5c832a06d88973f", "work_id": "arxiv:2610.41482"}], "version_id": "arxiv:2610.41482:v1:metadata-e5c832a06d88973f", "warnings": [], "work_id": "arxiv:2610.41482"}], "stage": "draft"}

messages.content: {"kind": "summary", "private_context": {"history": false, "notes": false, "profile": false}, "sources": [{"complete": true, "content_hash": "sha256:d3957979392138a48583d19fbe4eacdd34a9c9b5a7be53c71e284e37a247a492", "material_id": "mat-37637e07527abf0d35a62bf375e4ad57", "offset_basis": "page-local Unicode code points; end exclusive", "page_count": null, "page_numbers": null, "parser_revision": "workspace-plain-text-v1", "quality": "text_extracted", "scope": "abstract", "source_hash": "sha256:57d828d72e965955c14487b74cfd406d58aeab909942be50c97cafac89d3ccae", "spans": [{"end": 1597, "material_id": "mat-37637e07527abf0d35a62bf375e4ad57", "page": null, "parser_revision": "workspace-plain-text-v1", "scope": "abstract", "section": "abstract", "source_hash": "sha256:57d828d72e965955c14487b74cfd406d58aeab909942be50c97cafac89d3ccae", "span_id": "span-61a1d0725d68ccf9dad4480109110d91", "start": 0, "text": "This study investigates the effectiveness of large pre-trained language models (LLMs) for knowledge entity relation extraction (KERE) from academic papers. Existing studies have examined individual types of LLM-based strategies and evaluated model performance using metrics such as precision and recall. To provide a broader evaluation, this study investigates multiple strategies, including closed-source LLM-based CoT prompting, LoRA-adapted open-source LLMs, LLM-enhanced small pre-trained language models (SLMs), and SLM-enhanced closed-source LLMs. In addition, this study introduces two strategies, namely SLM-enhanced open-source LLMs and closed-source LLM-enhanced open-source LLMs. These strategies are evaluated from multiple perspectives, including metrics, their ability to mitigate errors observed in SLMs, and potential directions for model optimization. This study manually constructs two annotated datasets in the NLP domain, covering Abstract and Full-Text datasets. Experimental results show that the LoRA-adapted T5 model achieves the highest macro F1 scores of 0.7408 and 0.7013 on the Abstract and Full-Text datasets, respectively. SLMs also benefit from LLM-generated entity descriptions under the LLM-enhanced SLM strategy. Error analysis further reveals that the effectiveness of LLM-based strategies in mitigating SLM errors varies across error types. Based on the identified limitations and error patterns of these strategies, several optimization directions are proposed. In addition, combining strategies with different error patterns further improves KERE performance.", "version_id": "arxiv:2610.41552:v1:metadata-1c364e8ae805a931", "work_id": "arxiv:2610.41552"}], "version_id": "arxiv:2610.41552:v1:metadata-1c364e8ae805a931", "warnings": [], "work_id": "arxiv:2610.41552"}], "stage": "draft"}

We conduct empirical evaluations of ReAct and state-of-the-art baselines on four diverse benchmarks:
question answering (HotPotQA, Yang et al., 2018), fact veriﬁcation (Fever, Thorne et al., 2018),
text-based game (ALFWorld, Shridhar et al., 2020b), and webpage navigation (WebShop, Yao
et al., 2022). For HotPotQA and Fever, with access to a Wikipedia API that the model can interact
with, ReAct outperforms vanilla action generation models while being competitive with chain-of-
thought reasoning (CoT) (Wei et al., 2022). The best approach overall is a combination of ReAct
and CoT that allows for the use of both internal knowledge and externally obtained information
during reasoning. On ALFWorld and WebShop, two or even one-shot ReAct prompting is able
to outperform imitation or reinforcement learning methods trained with 103 ∼105 task instances,
with an absolute improvement of 34% and 10% in success rates respectively. We also demonstrate
the importance of sparse, versatile reasoning in decision making by showing consistent advantages
over controlled baselines with actions only. Besides general applicability and performance boost,
the combination of reasoning and acting also contributes to model interpretability, trustworthiness,
and diagnosability across all domains, as humans can readily distinguish information from model’s
internal knowledge versus external environments, as well as inspect reasoning traces to understand
the decision basis of model actions.

To summarize, our key contributions are the following: (1) we introduce ReAct, a novel prompt-
based paradigm to synergize reasoning and acting in language models for general task solving; (2) we
perform extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks to showcase the advantage of ReAct in a
few-shot learning setup over prior approaches that perform either reasoning or action generation in
isolation; (3) we present systematic ablations and analysis to understand th", "version_id": "arxiv:2210.03629:v3", "work_id": "arxiv:2210.03629"}, {"end": 4000, "material_id": "mat-2b7a38f3cfa1449f7728f044688ca2c2", "page": 3, "parser_revision": "workspace-pymupdf-1.28.0-text-sort-v1-selected-pages-v1", "scope": "excerpt", "section": null, "source_hash": "sha256:f285b0971ae4a790e402fb93966bed3adde2cf0a04977d08b2b40d6ab0cace69", "span_id": "span-e938044ecb931aff97360bd1fe27f3df", "start": 2000, "text": "e importance of acting in
reasoning tasks, and reasoning in interactive tasks; (4) we analyze the limitations of ReAct under the
prompting setup (i.e. limited support of reasoning and acting behaviors), and perform initial ﬁnetuning
experiments showing the potential of ReAct to improve with additional training data. Scaling up
ReAct to train and operate on more tasks and combining it with complementary paradigms like
reinforcement learning could further unlock the potential of large language models.

2  REAC T: SYNERGIZING REASONING + ACTING

Consider a general setup of an agent interacting with an environment for task solving. At time
step t, an agent receives an observation ot ∈O from the environment and takes an action at ∈A
following some policy π(at|ct), where ct = (o1, a1, · · · , ot−1, at−1, ot) is the context to the agent.
Learning a policy is challenging when the mapping ct 7→at is highly implicit and requires extensive
computation. For example, the agent shown in Figure 1(1c) is unable to generate the correct ﬁnal
action (Act 4) to ﬁnish the QA task as it requires complex reasoning over the trajectory context
(Question, Act 1-3, Obs 1-3). Similarly, the agent shown in Figure 1(2a) fails to comprehend from the
context that sinkbasin 1 does not contain peppershaker 1, thus keep producing hallucinating actions.
The idea of ReAct is simple: we augment the agent’s action space to Aˆ = A ∪L, where L is the
space of language. An action ˆat ∈L in the language space, which we will refer to as a thought or a
reasoning trace, does not affect the external environment, thus leading to no observation feedback.
Instead, a thought ˆat aims to compose useful information by reasoning over the current context ct,
and update the context ct+1 = (ct, ˆat) to support future reasoning or acting. As shown in Figure 1,
there could be various types of useful thoughts, e.g. decomposing task goals and create action plans
(2b, Act 1; 1d, Thought 1), injecting commonsense knowledge rele", "version_id": "arxiv:2210.03629:v3", "work_id": "arxiv:2210.03629"}, {"end": 5255, "material_id": "mat-2b7a38f3cfa1449f7728f044688ca2c2", "page": 3, "parser_revision": "workspace-pymupdf-1.28.0-text-sort-v1-selected-pages-v1", "scope": "excerpt", "section": null, "source_hash": "sha256:f285b0971ae4a790e402fb93966bed3adde2cf0a04977d08b2b40d6ab0cace69", "span_id": "span-e505ce9b7c0a17016f4e22e8caea7810", "start": 4000, "text": "vant to task solving (2b, Act 1),
extracting important parts from observations (1d, Thought2, 4), track progress and transit action plans
(2b, Act 8), handle exceptions and adjust action plans (1d, Thought 3), and so on.

However, as the language space L is unlimited, learning in this augmented action space is difﬁcult
and requires strong language priors. In this paper, we mainly focus on the setup where a frozen
large language model, PaLM-540B (Chowdhery et al., 2022)1, is prompted with few-shot in-context
examples to generate both domain-speciﬁc actions and free-form language thoughts for task solving
(Figure 1 (1d), (2b)). Each in-context example is a human trajectory of actions, thoughts, and
environment observations to solve a task instance (see Appendix C). For the tasks where reasoning is
of primary importance (Figure 1(1)), we alternate the generation of thoughts and actions so that the
task-solving trajectory consists of multiple thought-action-observation steps. In contrast, for decision
making tasks that potentially involve a large number of actions (Figure 1(2)), thoughts only need to

   1We show some GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020) results in Appendix A.1, which outperforms PaLM-540B.

messages.content: {"kind": "summary", "private_context": {"history": false, "notes": false, "profile": false}, "sources": [{"complete": true, "content_hash": "sha256:a1e2d03e8e9d1c84b615b075c16a309c69499e3fa466b8502a8ae63cc36aca32", "material_id": "mat-54f2f6e0645f499458d5030d06e35a59", "offset_basis": "page-local Unicode code points; end exclusive", "page_count": null, "page_numbers": null, "parser_revision": "workspace-plain-text-v1", "quality": "text_extracted", "scope": "abstract", "source_hash": "sha256:2b307ec864315d90d5e828786c2505fff1feda8837559b7e8601961ea9717759", "spans": [{"end": 875, "material_id": "mat-54f2f6e0645f499458d5030d06e35a59", "page": null, "parser_revision": "workspace-plain-text-v1", "scope": "abstract", "section": "abstract", "source_hash": "sha256:2b307ec864315d90d5e828786c2505fff1feda8837559b7e8601961ea9717759", "span_id": "span-3fd278aadaa92873179ed21c075ab368", "start": 0, "text": "Recursive textual memory can carry earlier errors into later updates, yet task performance alone does not establish memory reliability. We define self-consistency bias as the persistence of incorrect claims already present in the incoming memory. We present KEEPER, a comparative analysis of four auxiliary objectives along information-content and update-sensitivity axes within a shared recursive interface, examining how supervision targets relate to agent performance. Among evaluated conditions, reward-related prediction achieve the highest task performance before and after offline reinforcement learning, outperforming joint supervision. A claim-level analysis of one baseline trajectory documents error persistence despite corrective observations. Together, these analyses motivate evaluating error persistence and valid-information retention alongside task outcomes.", "version_id": "arxiv:2610.41482:v1:metadata-e5c832a06d88973f", "work_id": "arxiv:2610.41482"}], "version_id": "arxiv:2610.41482:v1:metadata-e5c832a06d88973f", "warnings": [], "work_id": "arxiv:2610.41482"}], "stage": "draft"}

messages.content: {"kind": "summary", "private_context": {"history": false, "notes": false, "profile": false}, "sources": [{"complete": true, "content_hash": "sha256:d3957979392138a48583d19fbe4eacdd34a9c9b5a7be53c71e284e37a247a492", "material_id": "mat-37637e07527abf0d35a62bf375e4ad57", "offset_basis": "page-local Unicode code points; end exclusive", "page_count": null, "page_numbers": null, "parser_revision": "workspace-plain-text-v1", "quality": "text_extracted", "scope": "abstract", "source_hash": "sha256:57d828d72e965955c14487b74cfd406d58aeab909942be50c97cafac89d3ccae", "spans": [{"end": 1597, "material_id": "mat-37637e07527abf0d35a62bf375e4ad57", "page": null, "parser_revision": "workspace-plain-text-v1", "scope": "abstract", "section": "abstract", "source_hash": "sha256:57d828d72e965955c14487b74cfd406d58aeab909942be50c97cafac89d3ccae", "span_id": "span-61a1d0725d68ccf9dad4480109110d91", "start": 0, "text": "This study investigates the effectiveness of large pre-trained language models (LLMs) for knowledge entity relation extraction (KERE) from academic papers. Existing studies have examined individual types of LLM-based strategies and evaluated model performance using metrics such as precision and recall. To provide a broader evaluation, this study investigates multiple strategies, including closed-source LLM-based CoT prompting, LoRA-adapted open-source LLMs, LLM-enhanced small pre-trained language models (SLMs), and SLM-enhanced closed-source LLMs. In addition, this study introduces two strategies, namely SLM-enhanced open-source LLMs and closed-source LLM-enhanced open-source LLMs. These strategies are evaluated from multiple perspectives, including metrics, their ability to mitigate errors observed in SLMs, and potential directions for model optimization. This study manually constructs two annotated datasets in the NLP domain, covering Abstract and Full-Text datasets. Experimental results show that the LoRA-adapted T5 model achieves the highest macro F1 scores of 0.7408 and 0.7013 on the Abstract and Full-Text datasets, respectively. SLMs also benefit from LLM-generated entity descriptions under the LLM-enhanced SLM strategy. Error analysis further reveals that the effectiveness of LLM-based strategies in mitigating SLM errors varies across error types. Based on the identified limitations and error patterns of these strategies, several optimization directions are proposed. In addition, combining strategies with different error patterns further improves KERE performance.", "version_id": "arxiv:2610.41552:v1:metadata-1c364e8ae805a931", "work_id": "arxiv:2610.41552"}], "version_id": "arxiv:2610.41552:v1:metadata-1c364e8ae805a931", "warnings": [], "work_id": "arxiv:2610.41552"}], "stage": "draft"}
